paragraphs: Blind signal separation asks how to recover individual sources from observations that mix them together. This paper develops an online learning algorithm for that problem when neither the original signals nor the mixing matrix is known. The number of sources is assumed to be available. Its guiding objective is to make the recovered outputs statistically less dependent on one another.

The algorithm measures dependence using average mutual information, which captures how much information outputs share. To evaluate this quantity, the authors use a Gram–Charlier expansion in place of an Edgeworth expansion. They then apply a natural gradient method to reduce it and introduce an activation function for the resulting online update.

The proposed rule has an equivariance property and can be implemented in a neural-network-like model. Computer simulations support its validity. The contribution brings together a statistical separation objective, an approximation for evaluating that objective, and an update suitable for learning as observations arrive.
neurips-1995-a-new-learning-algorithm-fo.tldr: An online signal-separation algorithm uses natural gradients to reduce mutual information between outputs when the sources and mixing matrix are unknown.

paragraphs: Movement control becomes difficult when sensory feedback arrives late and motor commands also take time to act. This paper proposes a hypothesis about how the cerebellum could help regulate movement despite both delays. The central idea is that a controller can learn to act in anticipation of what will happen without explicitly forecasting the sensory input it will receive.

The authors demonstrate the idea with a simplified cerebellar model controlling the endpoint position of a nonlinear spring–mass system. The setup includes realistic delays in the pathways carrying sensory information and outgoing commands. The model learns to regulate movement using input patterns that include the delayed feedback.

Prediction therefore appears in the controller's responses: it reacts early enough to influence subsequent movement. This differs from building a forward model of the controlled system to predict future sensory observations. The result supports an alternative computational account of cerebellar involvement in delayed control, demonstrated through learned positioning in the simplified mechanical system.
neurips-1995-a-predictive-switching-mode.tldr: A simplified cerebellar model learns anticipatory movement control despite feedback delays without explicitly predicting future sensory input.

paragraphs: This paper studies whether an adaptive version of back-propagation can train a network faster than ordinary gradient descent. The setting is online learning in two-layer neural networks, with the analysis allowing an arbitrary number of hidden units. The comparison concerns both the progress of training and the approach to optimal generalization.

The authors use a statistical mechanics framework and support their conclusions with numerical studies and rigorous analysis. A central finding concerns symmetry between hidden units. When units behave similarly, learning must differentiate their roles; the adaptive method breaks this symmetry more efficiently than standard back-propagation. This gives a specific explanation for its faster training.

The adaptive method also reaches optimal generalization more quickly in the studied setting. That result connects the speed of internal differentiation to performance beyond the training examples. The paper's contribution is therefore both comparative and explanatory: it identifies an advantage of the adaptive rule and links that advantage to how hidden units become distinct during learning.
neurips-1995-adaptive-back-propagation-i.tldr: Adaptive back-propagation speeds online learning by differentiating hidden units more efficiently and converging faster to optimal generalization.

paragraphs: This paper approaches facial-expression analysis through the muscle actions that produce visible facial changes. It uses the Facial Action Coding System as the basis for detecting and classifying these actions. The authors assembled more than 1,100 image sequences from 24 people performing over 150 individual actions or combinations, providing material for studying this task.

Three approaches extract different kinds of evidence. One analyzes overall graylevel appearance using principal components. Another explicitly measures local details, such as wrinkles. The third matches templates using motion flow fields, drawing on how the face changes across images. Together, they compare broad appearance, localized features, and movement as sources of classification information.

On a dataset covering six individual actions and 20 subjects, performance on new subjects was 89%, 57%, and 85%, respectively. Combining the approaches increased performance to 92%. This improvement indicates that their information was complementary in that evaluation. The reported comparison applies to the six-action subset, while the larger collection includes many more actions and combinations.
neurips-1995-classifying-facial-action-9.tldr: Combining overall appearance, local features, and facial motion improved classification of six facial actions on new subjects to 92%.

paragraphs: Visual processing often requires choosing a portion of the available information for further analysis. This paper addresses how that choice can be controlled in primates. It treats attention as a spatially bounded region of the visual field, or focus of attention, that moves through a scene according to the incoming information and the subject's attentional state.

The proposed model uses a saliency map to control this focus. Such a map provides a spatial representation for deciding where attention should be directed. This makes the selection of a location an explicit part of the visual-processing system: before higher-level analysis proceeds, the controller determines which region receives further processing.

The work presents this mechanism as an account of biological visual attention and as a potentially useful component of machine vision. Its significance lies in connecting scene analysis with control over where analysis occurs. The abstract frames understanding complex scenes as depending on this selection process and proposes the model as a way to study that relationship.
neurips-1995-control-of-selective-visual.tldr: A saliency-map model controls where visual attention moves, linking spatial selection to biological and machine scene understanding.

paragraphs: Nearest-neighbor classification relies on nearby examples having roughly similar class probabilities. In high-dimensional spaces, a neighborhood can cross regions where those probabilities change, introducing bias. This paper proposes adapting the shape of each neighborhood to the local classification problem, so that proximity reflects the directions that matter for distinguishing classes.

The method uses local linear discriminant analysis to estimate a distance measure. Information about class centroids determines local decision boundaries. Neighborhoods are then narrowed across those boundaries and stretched along them. This geometry aims to collect examples from directions where class membership changes less while limiting movement in directions where it changes more.

Once the neighborhoods have been reshaped, a neighborhood-based classifier can operate on them. The adaptation thus changes which examples count as nearby without requiring a single specific classifier afterward. The authors also propose combining local dimensional information into a global dimension-reduction method and describe how the techniques can extend to regression.
neurips-1995-discriminant-adaptive-neare.tldr: Locally learned distance measures reshape neighborhoods around decision boundaries to address high-dimensional nearest-neighbor bias.

paragraphs: A learning curve describes how learning performance changes as more examples become available. This paper investigates a modified VC formalism for producing such curves, focusing on how to evaluate the parameters that depend on the particular model. That focus matters because a general theoretical framework must connect to individual learning systems before it can describe their behavior.

The authors work through two examples: a two-dimensional homogeneous perceptron and a one-dimensional higher-order neuron. Both receive theoretical solutions, and the resulting learning curves are compared with their true learning curves. These examples provide concrete cases in which to examine the framework's model-specific calculations.

The stated finding is that the formalism can potentially represent several kinds of learning behavior, including curves with phase transitions. Here, the important distinction is between gradual change and a more abrupt shift in learning behavior. The examples show the framework's expressive potential, rather than restricting its predictions to one uniform shape of improvement.
neurips-1995-examples-of-learning-curves.tldr: Two theoretically solved neuron models illustrate how a modified VC framework can generate varied learning curves, including phase transitions.

paragraphs: This paper separates learning a dynamical system into choosing its structure and estimating its parameters. The goal is to construct systems with desired qualitative behavior and then train them to follow a desired trajectory. This makes model selection part of the design problem, rather than leaving all desired behavior to emerge from parameter adjustment.

The approach uses a decomposition of an n-dimensional nonlinear dynamical system into one gradient system and n minus one Hamiltonian systems. The designer selects these portions so that the intended behavior is obtainable. The decomposition therefore supplies a structured way to build the model before learning its numerical parameters.

For parameter estimation, the authors present a learning rule with a stable-convergence guarantee. They state that it converges to the desired system trajectory for all initial conditions and system inputs. Within this construction, the result provides a route to neural network models guaranteed to solve trajectory learning, connecting a deliberately chosen dynamical structure with a provably convergent training process.
neurips-1995-gradient-and-hamiltonian-dy.tldr: A gradient–Hamiltonian decomposition supports dynamical model design together with a learning rule guaranteed to converge to desired trajectories.

paragraphs: Learning to reproduce a song involves both recognizing its sound patterns and learning how to produce them. This paper models that connection in the song sparrow. Its computational system learns to categorize different song syllables and then uses those learned categories to train its own song production.

The perceptual part uses competitive learning to explore how organization might arise in a particular nucleus of the bird brain. This addresses the formation of the categories that guide behavior, supplying a computational account of perception alongside an account of production. The resulting categories become a basis for learning to reproduce the song.

Reinforcement learning links this perceptual organization to production. The model reproduces the song-production results of an earlier model while showing how learned perception can guide that process. Its main contribution is the connection between the two learning problems: organizing heard syllables provides useful structure for acquiring the actions needed to produce them, within a single computational explanation of song learning.
neurips-1995-how-perception-guides-produ.tldr: A song-sparrow model learns syllable categories and uses them to guide song production through reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: The paper examines an apparent puzzle in reading. The optical character recognition systems it discusses classify individual characters, while people can process long character strings during a single eye fixation. Recognizing several characters together appears to create a much larger classification problem, yet human reading handles this input in parallel.

The proposed explanation is that readers do not face every possible image of every possible string. Consistent, suitably placed eye fixations reduce the variety of visual inputs that need to be classified. Regularities in character sequences further reduce the effective range of patterns. These two sources of structure make the task more constrained than its raw dimensionality suggests.

The argument links eye placement and sequence structure to the difficulty of learning visual classifications. It suggests that the reading system's success depends partly on how its inputs are organized before and during recognition. The contribution is an explanation of how a seemingly high-dimensional task may become manageable through regularities in viewing and in the material being read.
neurips-1995-human-reading-and-the-curse.tldr: Consistent eye fixations and character-sequence regularities may make parallel recognition of long strings manageable for human readers.

paragraphs: Fourier transforms of Boolean functions have been useful for proving that certain learning problems can be solved. This paper asks whether those techniques can also support a practical learning algorithm. Its focus is the transition from a mathematically useful method to an implementation whose predictions and performance make it useful in practice.

The authors describe changes to the algorithm that they identify as crucial to its performance. According to the abstract, removing these changes would cause substantial deterioration. This places implementation choices at the center of the contribution: the practical behavior depends on how the Fourier-based learning procedure is realized, alongside the theoretical justification for using it.

Another contribution is a confidence level attached to each prediction, intended to measure how likely that prediction is to be correct. This gives the output an additional interpretation beyond the predicted answer itself. Together, the implementation changes and confidence estimates support the paper's case for Fourier techniques as an operational learning method.
neurips-1995-implementation-issues-in-th.tldr: Implementation changes and per-prediction confidence estimates help turn Fourier-based Boolean learning into a practical algorithm.

paragraphs: This paper asks how much information a neuron can transmit if the precise timing of each spike carries meaning. That hypothesis provides an upper-bound perspective on neural information coding. The authors develop a general way to quantify this information and apply it to a leaky integrate-and-fire model.

The calculation uses the distribution of intervals between spikes, assuming that spike times are measured with arbitrary but finite temporal resolution. Without added noise, all variation in those intervals can potentially carry information. Under that condition, the entropy of the interval distribution gives information per spike, and multiplying by the spike rate gives information per unit time.

The approach also supports experimental estimates where stimulus-reconstruction methods yield an uninformative lower bound. Preliminary recordings from hippocampal neurons in slices, driven by current injected into the cell body, suggest values as high as 6.3 bits per spike. These pilot findings concern information available under the timing-based hypothesis, making the treatment of timing and noise central to their interpretation.
neurips-1995-information-through-a-spiki.tldr: An interspike-interval framework quantifies timing-based neural information, with pilot recordings suggesting up to 6.3 bits per spike.

paragraphs: This paper proposes spending learning effort in advance so that later adaptation can be rapid. Its hierarchical system uses Parameterized Self-Organizing Maps to acquire context-dependent skills. During an initial investment stage, it learns a collection of basis mappings for representative contexts, specializing itself for a restricted range of future situations.

When a new context appears, the system adapts by interpolating among these learned mappings. The earlier learning therefore supplies the structure needed for the new skill. Rapid adaptation follows from working in the space of existing skills, where a new mapping can be assembled from the basis already acquired.

The demonstration uses a Puma robot and two cameras to learn a three-dimensional visuomotor mapping. It includes forward and backward relationships among end-effector positions, the two cameras' image coordinates, and six joint angles. After the investment phase, a single observation suffices to learn the transformation for a new camera setup. That result illustrates how prior specialization can sharply reduce the observations needed for later adaptation.
neurips-1995-investment-learning-with-hi.tldr: A hierarchy of previously learned mappings lets a robot adapt its visuomotor transformation to a new camera setup from one observation.

paragraphs: Tasks with long-term dependencies require a network to retain information that becomes useful much later. Gradient descent can struggle to train recurrent networks for such tasks. This paper examines whether choosing a NARX architecture makes that difficulty more manageable, building on earlier reports of more effective learning than in recurrent networks with hidden states.

The authors investigate NARX networks as a class with strong representational capabilities. Their central conclusion separates improvement from elimination of the problem: these networks still encounter long-term dependency difficulties, but their performance can be substantially better. Architecture therefore affects how severe the learning challenge becomes even when gradient-based training remains in use.

The reported experiments show that NARX networks can often retain information for two to three times as long as conventional recurrent networks. This is a comparative finding about the duration of useful memory in the studied tasks. It supports NARX networks as a way to extend that duration while preserving the paper's explicit conclusion that the underlying difficulty remains.
neurips-1995-learning-long-term-dependen.tldr: NARX networks can retain information two to three times longer than conventional recurrent networks without eliminating long-term dependency difficulties.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to discover the features underlying judgments of similarity. It uses the additive clustering model, in which two stimuli are similar to the extent that they share features. Each common feature contributes a weight, and the combined contributions determine the modeled similarity.

The authors propose a statistically motivated algorithm for learning this structure, drawing inspiration from unsupervised models with multiple causes. The task is to uncover a feature organization that accounts for the similarities among stimuli. Because several shared features can contribute to a pair's similarity, the model can describe structure through overlapping contributions.

The proposed algorithm promises simpler concepts, greater practical efficiency, and better solutions than earlier approaches to the model. The paper presents preliminary results on artificial data and two established similarity datasets. These results explore the proposed learning procedure in both constructed and existing examples. The contribution is a new route to fitting an interpretable account of similarity in terms of weighted shared features.
neurips-1995-learning-the-structure-of-s.tldr: A statistically motivated additive-clustering algorithm learns weighted shared features that explain similarities among stimuli.

paragraphs: This paper presents hardware for locating the largest or smallest signal among multiple inputs. Its key component is a neuron-like transistor called Neuron MOS. The circuits operate continuously in time, allowing the winning input to be tracked as signals change and supporting parallel processing for sorting multiple values.

The authors develop two circuit schemes. One uses an ensemble of ring oscillators with self-loop selection, where the winning location becomes an oscillating node. The other uses variable-threshold inverters driven by a shared ramp voltage. In that design, competitive excitation identifies winners, and a sequence of winner searches performs sorting.

The two schemes express selection through circuit dynamics: oscillation marks a winner in one, while responses to the common voltage ramp organize competition in the other. Test circuits were fabricated using a double-polysilicon CMOS process, and their operation was experimentally verified. The contribution therefore includes physical implementations of the proposed architectures, connecting continuous-time winner selection with demonstrated electronic behavior.
neurips-1995-neuron-mos-temporal-winner-.tldr: Two experimentally verified Neuron MOS circuit designs perform continuous-time winner selection and support parallel sorting.

paragraphs: Models of self-organizing cortical maps need to represent changes on different time scales. Neural activity changes quickly, while modifications to synaptic connections proceed more slowly. This paper treats those fast and slow processes together in a competitive neural system, reflecting the need to account for both short-term and long-term aspects of memory.

The authors construct a quadratic-type Lyapunov function for the system's dynamics. A Lyapunov function provides a mathematical way to assess stability by examining a quantity along the system's evolution. Here, the function addresses a model whose changing variables include both rapid neural responses and slower synaptic adaptation.

The paper also derives consequences of the stability analysis for network parameters. This connects an abstract mathematical construction to choices in the neural model: parameter settings matter for the behavior of the coupled processes. The contribution is a stability-analysis tool for a system in which activity and learning evolve together, rather than being treated as unrelated parts of cortical self-organization.
neurips-1995-quadratic-type-lyapunov-fun.tldr: A quadratic-type Lyapunov function analyzes stability in competitive networks coupling fast neural activity with slow synaptic changes.

paragraphs: This paper proposes recurrent neural networks that feed information back into their input units to handle incomplete observations. The approach covers static records with missing variables and sequential data in which variables are missing or observed at different frequencies. These cases share a practical issue: the network cannot always receive a complete set of fresh inputs.

The feedback mechanism allows missing inputs to be filled in as part of the learning system. The objective is discriminative: the filled values are chosen to help minimize a learning criterion, such as error at the output. Their role is therefore defined by the task the network is trained to perform.

This differs from estimating a conditional probability distribution for missing variables given observed ones. The paper's approach centers the quality of the eventual prediction or other learning objective. That distinction matters because it connects completion directly to task performance. The same recurrent arrangement provides a proposed framework for both gaps in static data and unequal observation schedules in sequences.
neurips-1995-recurrent-neural-networks-f.tldr: Input-feedback recurrent networks fill missing or asynchronous inputs according to the learning task's objective.

paragraphs: This paper studies reinforcement learning through approximations to the Q function. In its cost-based formulation, Q describes the expected discounted cost of choosing an action in a state and behaving optimally afterward. Knowing this function makes action selection straightforward: choose the action with the smallest Q value.

The setting is a Markov decision process with finite state and action sets. The next state and immediate cost depend on the current state and chosen action, and costs have finite mean and variance. The paper focuses on online learning, where the agent obtains knowledge by interacting with the environment instead of starting with its complete model.

The authors motivate Q-approximation algorithms and present new convergence results for two of them. These results address the mathematical behavior of learning procedures that use fitted approximations. The supplied discussion also distinguishes learning an environment model first from learning Q directly, placing the convergence contribution within the broader problem of deriving effective decisions from interaction.
neurips-1995-stable-fitted-reinforcement.tldr: The paper establishes convergence results for two reinforcement-learning algorithms that approximate the Q function.

paragraphs: This paper uses multilayer feedforward neural networks to predict a stock's excess return from its exposure to technical and fundamental factors. The prediction problem combines several descriptions of a stock into one estimated return outcome. The nonlinear model provides a way to relate those factor exposures to the quantity used for stock selection.

The evaluation connects the forecasts to a portfolio. The authors construct a hedged portfolio with equal amounts of capital allocated to long and short positions. This turns the modeling approach into a concrete investment arrangement whose historical returns can be examined, rather than assessing the prediction model only in isolation.

The portfolio's historical returns are compared with Treasury-bill returns and the S&P 500 index. These comparisons frame the demonstration around investment outcomes from the proposed approach. The abstract describes this evaluation as demonstrating effectiveness but supplies no numerical return comparison. Its stated contribution is the combination of nonlinear factor-based prediction, a balanced long–short portfolio, and historical benchmarking.
neurips-1995-stock-selection-via-nonline.tldr: Neural networks predict stock excess returns from multiple factors, with the approach evaluated through a hedged portfolio's historical returns.

paragraphs: This paper develops a geometric account of eye rotations, with particular attention to saccades. It brings different mathematical descriptions of rotation into a common framework using Lie group theory and differential geometry. This helps relate coordinate choices that otherwise describe the same movement in different forms.

The authors compute transformations between coordinate systems using the Campbell–Baker–Hausdorff formula. They then express Listing's law through the rotation Lie algebra so(3). This representation reveals a direct connection to Donders' law: the allowed eye orientations are described by the quotient space SO(3)/SO(2), which is equivalent to a sphere.

That sphere is precisely the space of gaze directions. The result therefore connects constraints on full eye orientation to the directions in which the eye can look. The paper's contribution is a unified mathematical framework for studying the oculomotor system and the relationship between these laws. The authors also identify the geometry of movements involving multiple arm joints as a possible extension.
neurips-1995-the-geometry-of-eye-rotatio.tldr: A geometric treatment connects Listing's and Donders' laws by relating constrained eye orientations to the sphere of gaze directions.

paragraphs: This paper explores prediction as a way for a sensory system to check its model of the environment. If the model captures useful structure, it should anticipate near-future input activity. Top-down connections allow those expectations to be compared with incoming signals, potentially biasing activity toward expected patterns and generating specific errors when predictions fail.

The author constructs a proof-of-concept layered network that predicts a simple moving stimulus. The model is event-driven and designed for computational efficiency. It also incorporates cortical-inspired features, including all-excitatory synapses and local inhibition, to investigate prediction within a particular kind of neural architecture.

After unsupervised learning, units respond to contour orientation and motion, as well as contour discontinuities and illusory contours. The significance is that learning to predict input produces sensitivity to several visual features, including ones beyond obvious stimulus properties. The demonstration links a temporal prediction task to the development of visual representations in the model, with the simple moving stimulus defining the reported setting.
neurips-1995-unsupervised-pixel-predicti.tldr: A network trained without supervision to predict a moving stimulus develops units sensitive to motion, contours, and illusory contours.

paragraphs: The paper connects two simple accounts of neuronal firing. A Poisson neuron generates random spikes according to a rate determined by the current stimulus. An integrate-and-fire neuron instead filters and accumulates its input until a threshold is reached, emits a spike, and resets. For a specified input, the latter model behaves deterministically.

The authors show how a slightly modified Poisson model can be derived from an integrate-and-fire neuron receiving a signal plus noise. The resulting relationship between stimulus and firing rate has a sigmoid shape described by an error function. Its shape depends on the variance of the input noise.

This result explains how stochastic firing can emerge from threshold-based dynamics when the inputs themselves fluctuate. It connects the rate-based description used in studies of neurons in living animals with a dynamical description used to conceptualize single-cell behavior. The equivalence concerns the modified Poisson model derived under noisy input, making noise part of the explanation for the relationship between the two descriptions.
neurips-1995-when-is-an-integrate-and-fi.tldr: Noisy inputs allow an integrate-and-fire neuron to yield a modified Poisson description with a noise-dependent sigmoid firing-rate function.

paragraphs: This paper compares gradient descent with a new Exponentiated Gradient algorithm for training a single neuron. It asks what guarantees can be made about their losses in the worst case. Although both methods can extend to larger networks, the proved bounds concern the single-neuron setting.

The central obstacle is that unwanted local minima complicate guarantees for gradient-based learning. The authors address it by pairing each strictly increasing, differentiable transfer function with a matching loss that prevents such minima. The identity transfer function pairs with squared loss, while the logistic sigmoid pairs with entropic loss. This choice links the neuron's response function to the objective used to train it.

With these pairings, the authors prove worst-case loss bounds for both algorithms. Differences in the structure of the bounds indicate an advantage for Exponentiated Gradient when many input components are irrelevant. The result explains a setting in which the choice of update rule matters, while grounding the comparison in a loss designed for the chosen transfer function.
neurips-1995-worst-case-loss-bounds-for-.tldr: Matching losses enable single-neuron worst-case guarantees that favor Exponentiated Gradient when inputs contain many irrelevant components.

paragraphs: This paper analyzes a Hebbian learning rule that includes a sigmoid nonlinearity. It studies the rule's stationary points to understand when learning develops a feature and when it suppresses weights. The analysis uses input variance as the measure of information content, making the strength of input variation central to the result.

When that variance is low, the weight vector converges to zero. Once the variance passes a threshold, the same rule begins learning a feature from the input automatically. This creates a transition between suppressing learning and extracting structure, governed by the input rather than a separate decision to activate learning.

Under certain conditions, the analysis suggests that the learned feature is the first principal component. The authors also show that the weight vector's length stays bounded when input variance is finite, and simulations confirm their theoretical results. Together, these findings describe both what the rule can learn and how its weights remain controlled as learning proceeds.
neurips-1996-hebb-learning-of-features-b.tldr: A sigmoid Hebbian rule suppresses weights for low-variance inputs and automatically learns a feature above a variance threshold.
